extracted.intended_audience: editors, researchers, funders, academic institutions and other stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and checklists to help stakeholders distinguish predatory (pseudo-)journals from legitimate scholarly journals by assessing editorial practices, transparency, indexing, fees, peer review, and other red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: predatory journals / pseudo-journals
rubrics_metrics.description: These entities prey on academicians for financial profit via article processing charges for open access articles, without meeting scholarly publishing standards; they may claim peer review and mimic legitimate journals but publish all or most submitted material without external peer review and do not follow standard policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predatory journals often solicit submissions widely, promise rapid publication, may collect fees without publishing, and fail to follow policies on archiving, conflicts of interest, errata, and transparency. 'Pseudo-journals' is an alternative name covering related behaviors (e.g., vanity journals, hijacked journals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to follow standard policies (archiving, COI, errata, transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not follow standard policies advocated by organizations such as WAME, COPE, ICMJE, and CSE regarding archiving of journal content, management of potential conflicts of interest, handling of errata, and transparency of journal processes and policies including fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit policies and adherence; absence or vagueness about these core practices is a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent unsolicited solicitation emails
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher sends frequent e-mails to large numbers of individuals soliciting manuscript submission and promising rapid publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulaic mass solicitations that do not specify interest in particular projects/areas increase suspicion; verify sender and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise of rapid publication / unrealistically short turnaround times
rubrics_metrics.description: Promised routine turnaround times for review and publication are so rapid that they seem 'too good to be true' and would be unlikely to encompass the time necessary for true peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid timelines alone are not definitive (some legitimate journals are fast), but combined with other red flags they are suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collects fees but does not publish or sends 'surprise' invoices
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides insufficient information or hides information about author fees, offering to publish an author’s paper and later sending an unanticipated 'surprise' invoice; in the most egregious cases they collect publication fees but the promised published articles never appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for clear, upfront fee policies and receipts; lack thereof is a strong red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims peer review but publishes without external peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Although predatory journals may claim to conduct peer review and mimic the structure of legitimate journals, they publish all or most submitted material without external peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of transparent peer review processes, editorial handling, and actual reviewer reports where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mention of peer review in Instructions for Authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is not mentioned in the Instructions for Authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of any explanation about peer review procedures is a warning sign (Table 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Little or no information about editor or editorial board
rubrics_metrics.description: Little or no information is provided regarding the editor or editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate journals typically identify editors with institutional affiliations and credentials; lack of such information warrants caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal location missing or inconsistent with editors' locations
rubrics_metrics.description: No location is listed for the journal offices, or location is very different than the location of the editors and editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check contact/address information and whether it aligns with editorial affiliations; mismatches (e.g., US PO box for an otherwise foreign operation) are suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website not easily discoverable in internet searches
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal website is not easily accessible in an internet search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New or legitimate journals in LMICs may be harder to find; use multiple indices and verify other indicators before concluding it's predatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusual publication volume patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal publishes either an unusually small, unusually large, or markedly variable numbers of articles each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme patterns in publication counts (very few, huge numbers, or erratic output) can indicate poor editorial control or mass-profit model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid promise of publication coupled with lack of editorial response
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not receive a response to e-mail or telephone messages sent to the editor or journal office within a few days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-responsiveness to queries is a red flag, especially when combined with promises of rapid processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal name imitates established journals
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of the journal is very similar to the name of a well-known, established journal with a good reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name mimicry/hijacking is used to deceive authors; verify ISSN, publisher, and indexing to distinguish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atypical publication fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication fees are atypical for the scholarly publishing industry (much higher or much lower fees can both signal problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider regional cost differences; very low fees are not proof of legitimacy, nor are very high fees without transparent justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficult to identify articles in databases
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to identify articles published in the journal when searching Google Scholar or other databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New journals may lag in indexing; false claims of indexing are different and suspicious (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing author affiliation/contact information in published articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about author affiliations and/or contact information is not present in published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate articles include author affiliations and contact details; absence reduces accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board members unaware of affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone you know listed on the editorial board or journal staff, when you query them about the journal, is unaware of their supposed affiliation with the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check editorial members’ personal/institutional pages for confirmation; false listings are explicit evidence of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor/publisher owner listed as editor of all journals
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher’s owner is identified as the editor of each and every journal published by the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests lack of independent editorial oversight and potential commercialized control of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single individual identified as specific journal’s editor
rubrics_metrics.description: No single individual is identified as any specific journal’s editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of clear editorial leadership prevents accountability and is suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal does not identify a formal editorial/review board
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal does not identify a formal editorial / review board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of a named editorial board is a key warning sign; verify names, roles, and affiliations when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: No academic information provided for editors/staff/reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: No academic information is provided regarding the editor, editorial staff, and/or review board members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of credentials or institutional affiliations suggests non-scholarly operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor/review board lacks academic expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence exists showing that the editor and/or review board members do not possess academic expertise to reasonably qualify them to be publication gatekeepers in the journal’s field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review board qualifications should align with the journal’s scope; lack of expertise undermines quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate editorial boards across journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more journals have duplicate editorial boards (i.e., same editorial board for more than one journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate boards across many titles suggest template-driven, low-quality operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient or fabricated editorial board membership
rubrics_metrics.description: The journals have an insufficient number of board members (e.g., 2 or 3 members), have concocted editorial boards (made up names), name scholars on their editorial board without their knowledge or permission or have board members who are prominent researchers but exempt them from any contributions to the journal except the use of their names and/or photographs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm board membership independently; honorary-only listings or fabricated names are strong evidence of predatory practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of geographical diversity on editorial board
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little or no geographical diversity among the editorial board members, especially for journals that claim to be international in scope or coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in interpreting this criterion for journals legitimately concentrated in a region; it was a controversial Beall criterion and may unfairly flag LMIC journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial board engages in gender bias (i.e., exclusion of any female members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gender imbalance can be an indicator of problematic practices but is not solely determinative of predatory status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of transparency in publishing operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates a lack of transparency in publishing operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent descriptions of policies, governance, fees, and processes are expected for legitimate journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: No policies or practices for digital preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Has no policies or practices for digital preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for archiving (e.g., CLOCKSS, Portico) or preservation statements; absence threatens the scholarly record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begins operations with a large fleet of templated journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Begins operations with a large fleet of journals, often using a common template to quickly create each journal’s home page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large number of low-effort titles created simultaneously can indicate a business model aimed at volume rather than quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocks indexing / prevents search engine crawling or locks PDFs
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not allow search engines to crawl the published content, preventing the content from being indexed in academic indexes; copy-proofs (locks) their PDFs, thus making it harder to check for plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate open access journals enable indexing and do not lock content that impedes scholarly use; PDF locking is unusual and problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal name incongruent with mission or origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a journal is incongruent with the journal’s mission or does not adequately reflect its origin (e.g., claiming 'Canadian' or 'Swiss' when no connection exists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misleading titles are used to feign credibility; check publisher and editorial affiliations for confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: False claims of impact factors / use of fake metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher falsely claims one or more of its journals have actual (Thomson-Reuters) impact factors, or advertises impact factors assigned by fake 'impact factor' services, or it uses some made up measure (e.g., view factor), feigning/claiming an exaggerated international standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify claimed metrics with official services (Clarivate/Journal Citation Reports) and beware of made-up indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spam peer review requests to unqualified reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher sends spam requests for peer reviews to scholars unqualified to review submitted manuscripts, in the sense that the specialties of the invited reviewers do not match the papers sent to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate reviewer selection should match manuscript subject matter; mismatches indicate poor editorial practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: False claims of indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher falsely claims to have its content indexed in legitimate abstracting and indexing services or claims that its content is indexed in resources that are not abstracting and indexing services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check indexing claims directly with the named services; false or inflated indexing claims are common in predatory operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient resources to prevent author misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher dedicates insufficient resources to preventing and eliminating author misconduct, to the extent that the journal or journals suffer from repeated cases of plagiarism, self-plagiarism, image manipulation, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for plagiarism-detection policies and evidence of corrections or retractions when misconduct is detected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses author-suggested reviewers without adequate vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher asks the corresponding author for suggested reviewers and the publisher subsequently uses the suggested reviewers without sufficiently vetting their qualifications or authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify reviewer identities and conflicts of interest; unvetted suggested reviewers can enable fake peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republishes previously published papers without credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-publish papers already published in other venues/outlets without providing appropriate credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-plagiarism and duplicate publication without citation are unethical; check DOI/original venue to confirm originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boastful marketing language claiming leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Use boastful language claiming to be a 'leading publisher' even though the publisher may only be a startup or a novice organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing hyperbole should be corroborated by independent indicators of quality (indexing, editorial board, publishing history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operates as vanity press with deceptive address
rubrics_metrics.description: Operate in a Western country chiefly for the purpose of functioning as a vanity press for scholars in a developing country (e.g., utilizing a mail drop address or PO box address in the United States, while actually operating from a developing country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm physical location, staff affiliations, and corporate registrations where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal or no copyediting / proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide minimal or no copyediting or proofreading of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High rates of typographical/grammatical errors in published articles suggest inadequate editorial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishes non-academic or pseudo-scientific material
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish papers that are not academic at all, e.g., essays by lay people, polemical editorials, or obvious pseudo-science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the journal's published content aligns with accepted scholarly standards for the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact page lacks verifiable contact/location information
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a 'contact us' page that only includes a web form or an email address, and the publisher hides or does not reveal its location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate publishers provide clear postal addresses, phone numbers, and other means to verify identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies other publishers' author guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher copies 'authors guidelines' verbatim (or with minor editing) from other publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarized policies indicate low editorial standards; check uniqueness of policies and whether they are appropriate to the journal's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient or misrepresented contact/headquarters information
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher lists insufficient contact information, including contact information that does not clearly state the headquarters location or misrepresents the headquarters location (e.g., through the use of addresses that are actually mail drops).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm corporate registration and physical office locations where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessively broad journal scope to attract submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher publishes journals that are excessively broad (e.g., Journal of Education) in order to attract more articles and gain more revenue from author fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very broad scopes that conflate unrelated areas may be a commercial strategy rather than legitimate disciplinary focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combines unrelated fields in one journal
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher publishes journals that combine two or more fields not normally treated together (e.g., International Journal of Business, Humanities and Technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdisciplinary journals exist legitimately, but arbitrary combinations designed to attract submissions are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charges fees while retaining copyright or requiring transfer at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher charges authors for publishing but requires transfer of copyright and retains copyright on journal content. Or the publisher requires the copyright transfer upon submission of manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate open access models typically allow authors to retain copyright and use standard licenses; be cautious of pre-submission transfer demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poorly maintained website (dead links, misspellings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher has poorly maintained websites, including dead links, prominent misspellings and grammatical errors on the website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Website quality alone is not definitive but pervasive errors reflect lack of editorial care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized use of licensed images
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher makes unauthorized use of licensed images on their website, taken from the open web, without permission or licensing from the copyright owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check image attributions and licensing; unauthorized use suggests disregard for intellectual property norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beall's criteria should not be sole determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Beall's list and criteria are a reasonable starting point but should not be used as the solitary method for determining whether a journal is predatory or legitimate because some criteria can misidentify legitimate journals (especially from LMICs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple indicators and contextual judgment; be aware of criticisms of particular criteria (e.g., geographic diversity) and the possibility of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ inclusion as positive indicator (but not definitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) is an indicator of quality; DOAJ indexes high quality, peer reviewed OA journals that use an appropriate quality control system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOAJ is helpful but not comprehensive and listing does not guarantee high quality; DOAJ has user mechanisms to report problematic journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ Seal criteria: provide permanent identifiers (e.g., DOIs)
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the DOAJ Seal, journals must provide permanent identifiers (e.g., DOIs) in the papers published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent identifiers facilitate citation and discovery; lack of DOIs is problematic for many fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ Seal criteria: provide DOAJ with article metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the DOAJ Seal, journals must provide DOAJ with article metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured metadata supports indexing and discovery; absence complicates evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ Seal criteria: deposit content with long-term digital preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the DOAJ Seal, journals must deposit content with a long term digital preservation or archiving program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of CLOCKSS, Portico, national libraries, or other preservation commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ Seal criteria: embed machine-readable CC licensing information
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the DOAJ Seal, journals must embed machine-readable CC licensing information in articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear machine-readable licensing enables lawful reuse and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ Seal criteria: allow generous reuse consistent with CC BY/CC BY-SA/CC BY-NC
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the DOAJ Seal, journals must allow generous reuse and mixing of content, in accordance with a CC BY, CC BY-SA or CC BY-NC license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check license statements and machine-readable tags to verify permitted reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ Seal criteria: have a deposit policy registered with a deposit policy registry
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the DOAJ Seal, journals must have a deposit policy registered with a deposit policy registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposit policies clarify author and repository rights; verify registry entries where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ Seal criteria: allow the author to hold the copyright without restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the DOAJ Seal, journals must allow the author to hold the copyright without restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-retained copyright with appropriate licensing is a hallmark of many legitimate OA journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Do you or your colleagues know the journal?
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether you or your colleagues are familiar with the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior knowledge or colleagues' experience is a practical early indicator but absence does not imply predatory status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Have you read any articles in the journal before?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you previously read articles published in the journal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the quality of published articles to judge suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Is it easy to discover the latest papers in the journal?
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you easily find the journal's latest papers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discoverability in searches and indexes supports legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Can you easily identify and contact the publisher?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the publisher clearly identifiable and contactable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent publisher identity and contact methods are expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Is the publisher name clearly displayed on the journal website?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the publisher name clearly displayed on the journal website?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hidden publisher names or ambiguous ownership are suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Can you contact the publisher by telephone, email, and post?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the publisher reachable via telephone, email, and postal address?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple modes of contact increase verifiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Is the journal clear about the type of peer review it uses?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the journal clearly state its peer review model (e.g., single-blind, double-blind, open)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear peer review descriptions and workflows are markers of journal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Are articles indexed in services that you use?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the journal's articles indexed in the databases and indexes familiar to you?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing in appropriate services supports discoverability and perceived legitimacy; verify claims directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Is it clear what fees will be charged?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is fee information clearly stated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent fee schedules and what they cover should be provided before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Does the journal site explain what these fees are for and when they will be charged?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the site explain purpose and timing of fees?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclear or hidden fee policies are a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Do you recognize the editorial board?
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you recognize the editorial board members?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizable, appropriately qualified board members are reassuring; verify via member websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Have you heard of the editorial board members?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you heard of the editorial board members?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with board members can indicate community standing; lack of recognition requires further checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Do the editorial board members mention the journal on their own websites?
rubrics_metrics.description: Do board members list their affiliation with the journal on their personal or institutional pages?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent confirmation from board members reduces risk of false listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Is the publisher a member of a recognized industry initiative?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the publisher belong to recognized industry initiatives (e.g., COPE)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership in COPE, OASPA, or similar indicates engagement with recognized standards; verify membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: If OA, is it listed in DOAJ?
rubrics_metrics.description: If the journal is open access, is it listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOAJ listing is a positive indicator but not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: If OA, does the publisher belong to OASPA?
rubrics_metrics.description: If open access, does the publisher belong to the Open Access Scholarly Publishers Association (OASPA)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership in trade associations suggests commitment to best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: Is the publisher a member of another trade association?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the publisher belong to other recognized trade associations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional memberships can bolster credibility; always verify claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME framework: use initial indicators then investigate further
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by assessing whether the journal has any of the characteristics Beall viewed as potentially problematic, its presence in the DOAJ, and presence of 'Think. Check. Submit.' features, with further investigation guided by these initial indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment remains subjective; review website and policies for 'warning sign' features and weigh the number/severity of red flags—the more red flags, the greater the suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME 'Warning Sign' — No information on author fees in Instructions for Authors
rubrics_metrics.description: No information as to whether there are author fees in the Instructions for Authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent fee policies must be present before submission; absence is a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME 'Warning Sign' — You have received formulaic email solicitations
rubrics_metrics.description: You or your colleagues have received formulaic e-mail solicitations for submissions that do not specify an interest in particular projects or areas that you are working on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic solicitations are a common predatory practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME 'Warning Sign' — Promised routine rapid turnaround times
rubrics_metrics.description: Promised routine turnaround times for review and publication are so rapid that they seem 'too good to be true' and would be unlikely to encompass the time necessary for true peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated: interpret in context of other features.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME 'Warning Sign' — No response to editor/journal office communications
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not receive a response to e-mail or telephone messages sent to the editor or journal office within a few days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of responsiveness is suspicious, especially in combination with other red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME 'Warning Sign' — Journal name similar to established journal
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of the journal is very similar to the name of a well-known, established journal with a good reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again, check ISSN and publisher to avoid being misled by name mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME 'Warning Sign' — Publication fees atypical
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication fees are atypical for the scholarly publishing industry (much higher or much lower fees can both signal problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider field norms and regional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME 'Warning Sign' — Hard to find articles in searches/databases
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to identify articles published in the journal when searching Google Scholar or other databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm indexing claims; new legitimate journals may have lags.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME 'Warning Sign' — Missing author affiliation/contact in articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about author affiliations and/or contact information is not present in published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces traceability and accountability for published work.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME recommendation: institutions should scrutinize quality as well as quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic institutions and funders should scrutinize the quality as well as the quantity of faculty publications, identifying acceptable journals according to quality criteria rather than excluding all online journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should develop context-sensitive policies and mentorship to help authors identify credible venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: WAME recommendation: do not rely solely on lists; enable correction and conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Future initiatives should be transparent and objective with mechanisms for journals incorrectly identified as predatory to correct the record and for predatory journals to become legitimate by improving their practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage remediation pathways and transparency in any blacklist/whitelist processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate multiple sources and aggregate red flags
rubrics_metrics.description: Because existing initiatives do not provide error-proof methods for determining journal status, individuals who aim to gain high assurance need to investigate further using WAME framework, DOAJ, Think.Check.Submit, Beall's indicators, and website/policy review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count and weigh 'warning sign' features; the more red flags present, the more hesitant one should be to consider the journal legitimate.
